title: Road Trip Rest Stop Calculator
description: Estimate how many rest stops a drive needs from its distance and your stop interval with the Road Trip Rest Stop Calculator. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, an 840-mile drive with a stop every 140 miles divides into six legs and five proper stops — the skeleton of a day that does not end in a daze.
quick_answer: The Road Trip Rest Stop Calculator divides a drive's distance by the interval at which you like to stop and tells you how many rest stops the journey contains. Enter trip distance and your interval — in miles or hours turned into miles — and plan around real breaks.

popular_table.title: Stops by distance and interval
popular_table.intro: Intermediate stops = (distance ÷ interval) − 1, rounded sensibly — the stops between departure and arrival.
popular_table.note: Counts treat the destination as the final stop. Your interval is a preference, not a law — weather, passengers and bladder diplomacy amend it.

faq: What does this tool calculate?
The number of intermediate rest stops in a drive: the distance divided into legs by your stop interval, minus the destination itself.
Do I need an account?
No. Distance and interval in, stops out.
Can I rely on this for professional work?
As a planning count, yes. Professional driving-hours law (tachograph rules, hours-of-service) is stricter and separate — this is the comfort arithmetic beneath it.
Does the route include live traffic?
No. Congestion argues for more stops, not fewer; the count is the calm-weather skeleton.
Why is road distance longer than straight-line?
Stops happen on roads. Count the road distance or the legs arrive later than planned.
How long should each stop be?
Long enough to walk, drink and reset — most drivers find 15–25 minutes restores rather than merely pauses. The count here is stops; their length is your craft.
My interval is in hours.
Multiply hours by your cruising speed to get the interval in miles (2 h × 65 mph = 130 mi), then use this page — or keep the plan in hours and count legs by the clock.
Stops for the dog count double?
They count once each and take longer — lengthen the stop budget, not the count. The calculator counts; the dog negotiates duration.
Scenic stops versus rest stops?
Both stop the wheels. Count them together for time, separately for sanity — the road does not care why you stopped.
Night driving — same intervals?
Most drivers shorten intervals after dark. The plan that survives the night is the shorter-legged one.
